cards.prose: Levi sits at the tax booth, a man the town had written off, and Yahusha (Jesus) stops at his seat and says *Follow me*. Ezekiel heard the shepherd promise to *seek that which was lost*, and here the seeking reaches a man at his work, and he gets up from his booth and goes after him.
cards.member_phrase: I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away
cards.member_sentence: Adonai Yahuah (the Lord GOD) promises to seek the lost and bring back the driven away, which is what happens when Yahusha (Jesus) calls Levi from his seat.

cards.prose: When the complaint about his company reaches him, he answers that the whole have no need of a physician, and that he came to call sinners to repentance. Ezekiel had charged the shepherds of Yashar'el (Israel) with leaving the sick unhealed and the lost unsought, and ruling the flock with force. Yahusha (Jesus) goes to the very sheep that charge describes.
cards.member_phrase: neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken
cards.member_sentence: Adonai Yahuah (the Lord GOD) charges the shepherds with leaving the sick unhealed and the broken unbound, the work Yahusha (Jesus) takes up among sinners.

cards.prose: He calls himself the bridegroom, and while the bridegroom is with them the guests cannot fast. Hosea had already told whose wedding this is: Yahuah (the LORD) says to the house he put away, *I will betroth thee unto me for ever*, in righteousness and in mercies. The gladness that keeps the guests from fasting is that promise being kept to the scattered house of Yashar'el (Israel).
cards.member_phrase: I will betroth thee unto me for ever
cards.member_sentence: Yahuah (the LORD) promises to betroth the house he put away to himself for ever, the wedding Yahusha (Jesus) steps into as the bridegroom.
cards.flag: The reading that the bride of Hosea 2 is the scattered house is the author's line; Mark 2:19 itself names only the bridegroom.

cards.prose: The disciples are hungry and pluck the ears as they go, and the charge is that this is not lawful on the sabbath. Leviticus shows how the Torah itself treats a field: the corners and the gleanings are left standing for the poor, so hunger in a field is something the commandments make room for, not something they forbid.
cards.member_phrase: thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field
cards.member_sentence: Leviticus leaves the corners and gleanings of the field for the poor and the stranger, so the Torah itself makes room for the hungry in a field.

cards.prose: This is the verse the disciples were living by. A man walking through his neighbour's standing corn may take the ears in his hand, only he may not put a sickle to it, and that is just what they did, ears by hand as they went. The charge against them rests on a rule laid over the day, not on the commandment about the day.
cards.member_phrase: then thou mayest pluck the ears with thine hand
cards.member_sentence: Moses allows a hungry man to pluck ears by hand in his neighbour's standing corn, which is exactly what the disciples were doing.

cards.prose: He sends them back to a page they all knew. David comes to Nob hungry with his men, and the priest tells him *There is no common bread under mine hand, but there is hallowed bread* (1 Samuel 21:4). The hungry men are fed from the bread that was set apart, by the priest who had it to give. That is the story Yahusha (Jesus) lays beside the disciples in the grain.
cards.member_phrase: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest
cards.member_sentence: David comes hungry to the priest at Nob, the story Yahusha (Jesus) names when the disciples are charged for plucking grain on the sabbath.
